incoming.explanation: John's absence from every surviving near-window passenger list is consistent with reception into an existing community rather than a documented shared crossing.
No Hingham reception-corridor record survives either, so the settlement pattern, not a transit record, is all the migration evidence can support.
The reception network fixes the mode of settlement but not the English origin; the corridor question is held to the identity work.
The land-and-neighbour network is the fuller evidence behind the reading of reception into an established community.

outgoing.explanation: The reception reading rests on the 1641 gunpowder-fines record that first places John among named Weymouth men.
The migration-mode conclusion synthesizes the Weymouth associate reading: John's 1641 co-petitioners and his residual creditor were established townsmen, not fellow newcomers.

finding.statement: John Gurney's migration reads as the reception of a newcomer into an already-established Weymouth community rather than arrival with a known emigration party: the men he is first grouped with in the 1641 gunpowder-fines record — James Ludden (an Old Planter by 1632) and Richard Porter (a 1635 Hull-company settler) — and his later Weymouth creditor John King were all settlers of a half-generation's standing, not fellow newcomers.
